dmm-2019-power-01a.title: Exhibit the dependence
dmm-2019-power-01a.body: $1\cdot(1,2,0)+2\cdot(1,-1,1)-1\cdot(3,0,2)=(1+2-3,\ 2-2-0,\ 0+2-2)=(0,0,0)$ with coefficients $1,2,-1$ not all zero. So the vectors are linearly dependent. ∎

dmm-2019-power-01b.title: Solve the system
dmm-2019-power-01b.body: Suppose $c_1(1,0,0)+c_2(0,1,1)+c_3(1,0,1)=0$. The coordinates give $c_1+c_3=0$, $c_2=0$, $c_2+c_3=0$. Then $c_2=0$, so $c_3=0$ and $c_1=0$. Hence the vectors are linearly independent. ∎

dmm-2019-power-01c.title: Standard basis
dmm-2019-power-01c.body: Let $e_i$ have $i$th coordinate $1$ and all other coordinates $0$. If $c_1e_1+\dots+c_ne_n=0$, the vector on the left is $(c_1,\dots,c_n)$, so all $c_i=0$. Hence $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are linearly independent. ∎

dmm-2019-power-02a.title: Exhibit the dependence
dmm-2019-power-02a.body: $1\cdot(1,2,1)+2\cdot(1,-1,1)-3\cdot(1,0,1)=(1+2-3,\ 2-2+0,\ 1+2-3)=(0,0,0)$, and the coefficients sum to $1+2-3=0$ and are not all zero. So the vectors are affinely dependent. ∎

dmm-2019-power-02b.title: Solve the system
dmm-2019-power-02b.body: Suppose $c_1(1,2,0)+c_2(1,-1,1)+c_3(3,0,2)=0$ and $c_1+c_2+c_3=0$. The coordinates give $c_1+c_2+3c_3=0$, $2c_1-c_2=0$, $c_2+2c_3=0$. Subtracting $c_1+c_2+c_3=0$ from the first gives $2c_3=0$, so $c_3=0$; then $c_2=0$ from the third and $c_1=0$ from the second. Hence the vectors are affinely independent. ∎

dmm-2019-power-03.title: Contrapositive
dmm-2019-power-03.body: Suppose $x_1,\dots,x_k$ are affinely dependent: there are $c_i$ not all zero with $\sum c_ix_i=0$ and $\sum c_i=0$. The first equation alone already shows that the vectors are linearly dependent. So linear independence implies affine independence. ∎

dmm-2019-power-04.title: Standard basis
dmm-2019-power-04.body: The standard basis vectors $e_1,\dots,e_n$ (with a $1$ in position $i$ and $0$ elsewhere) are linearly independent, since $\sum c_ie_i=(c_1,\dots,c_n)=0$ forces every $c_i=0$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-05a.title: Origin and basis
dmm-2019-power-05a.body: Take $x_0=0$ and $x_i=e_i$ for $i=1,\dots,n$. Suppose $c_0x_0+c_1e_1+\dots+c_ne_n=0$ and $c_0+\dots+c_n=0$. The vector equation gives $(c_1,\dots,c_n)=0$, and then $c_0=-(c_1+\dots+c_n)=0$. So all coefficients vanish and the $n+1$ vectors are affinely independent. ∎

dmm-2019-power-05b.title: Lift to one dimension higher
dmm-2019-power-05b.body: Suppose $x_1,\dots,x_k\in\mathbb R^n$ are affinely independent. Put $y_i=(x_i,1)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$ (append a coordinate $1$). Then $\sum c_iy_i=0$ means exactly $\sum c_ix_i=0$ and $\sum c_i=0$. Since the $x_i$ are affinely independent this forces all $c_i=0$, i.e. $y_1,\dots,y_k$ are linearly independent in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. At most $n+1$ vectors in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ are linearly independent, so $k\le n+1$. Together with part (a) (which gives $n+1$ affinely independent vectors), the maximum is $n+1$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-06.title: The diagonals
dmm-2019-power-06.body: Let $A=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}$ and $B=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$. The convex hull of $A$ is the diagonal segment from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, and that of $B$ the other diagonal. They meet at $p=(\frac12,\frac12)=\frac12(0,0)+\frac12(1,1)=\frac12(1,0)+\frac12(0,1)$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-07a.title: Affine dependence
dmm-2019-power-07a.body: Since $n+2>n+1$, the vectors $x_1,\dots,x_{n+2}$ cannot be affinely independent, so by definition there are $c_i$ not all zero with $\sum c_ix_i=0$ and $\sum c_i=0$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-07b.title: Contradiction
dmm-2019-power-07b.body: If $I$ were empty then all $c_i\le0$. Since $\sum c_i=0$, a sum of nonpositive numbers equal to $0$ forces every $c_i=0$, contradicting that the $c_i$ are not all zero. So $I\ne\emptyset$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-07c.title: Split the zero sum
dmm-2019-power-07c.body: $I$ and $J$ partition $\{1,\dots,n+2\}$, so $\sum_{i\in I}c_i+\sum_{j\in J}c_j=\sum c_i=0$, i.e. $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{j\in J}(-c_j)$. Since $I$ is nonempty and each $c_i>0$ there, $\sum_{i\in I}c_i>0$, so the common sum is nonzero (positive). ∎

dmm-2019-power-07d.title: Normalize
dmm-2019-power-07d.body: From $\sum_{\text{all}}c_ix_i=0$ and the partition $I\sqcup J$ we get $\sum_{i\in I}c_ix_i=\sum_{j\in J}(-c_j)x_j$. Let $s=\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{j\in J}(-c_j)>0$ and define $p=\sum_{i\in I}\frac{c_i}{s}x_i=\sum_{j\in J}\frac{-c_j}{s}x_j$. The weights $\frac{c_i}s$ ($i\in I$) are positive with sum $1$, and the weights $\frac{-c_j}{s}$ ($j\in J$) are nonnegative with sum $1$. So $p$ lies in the convex hull of $A$ and in the convex hull of $B$. As $I\ne\emptyset$ and $s>0$ forces $J\ne\emptyset$, and $I,J$ are disjoint, this proves Radon's Theorem. ∎

dmm-2019-power-08a.title: Radon point
dmm-2019-power-08a.body: By Radon's Theorem (the proof works for indexed families, so repeated points are fine) there is a partition $\{1,\dots,n+2\}=I\sqcup J$ and a point $p$ in the convex hull of $\{x_i:i\in I\}$ and of $\{x_j:j\in J\}$. Fix any index $m$. If $m\in I$, then every $x_j$ with $j\in J$ lies in $X_m$ (as $j\ne m$), so by convexity the convex hull of $\{x_j:j\in J\}$ lies in $X_m$; hence $p\in X_m$. If $m\in J$, use $\{x_i:i\in I\}$ in the same way. So $p\in X_m$ for every $m$, i.e. $p\in\bigcap X_i$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-08b.title: Induction on $k$
dmm-2019-power-08b.body:
The case $k=n+2$ is the previous part. Suppose the theorem holds for some $k\ge n+2$ and let $X_1,\dots,X_{k+1}$ be convex sets any $n+1$ of which intersect. Consider the $k$ convex sets $X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},X_k\cap X_{k+1}$ (the intersection of convex sets is convex). Any $n+1$ of these have a common point: if none of the chosen sets is $X_k\cap X_{k+1}$ this is the hypothesis. Otherwise the chosen sets are $X_{i_1},\dots,X_{i_n},X_k\cap X_{k+1}$. The $n+2$ sets $X_{i_1},\dots,X_{i_n},X_k,X_{k+1}$ have the property that any $n+1$ of them intersect, so by the case $k=n+2$ they have a common point, which lies in all of the chosen sets.

By the induction hypothesis the $k$ sets $X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},X_k\cap X_{k+1}$ have a common point, and that point lies in all of $X_1,\dots,X_{k+1}$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-09.title: Helly for disks
dmm-2019-power-09.body: If $k\le3$ there is nothing to prove, so let $k\ge4$ and let the points be $x_1,\dots,x_k$. Let $D_i$ be the closed disk of radius $1$ centered at $x_i$; these are convex. For any three points $x_i,x_j,x_l$ there is a unit disk with center $q$ containing them, so $|q-x_i|,|q-x_j|,|q-x_l|\le1$, i.e. $q\in D_i\cap D_j\cap D_l$. So any three of the disks intersect, and Helly's Theorem in $\mathbb R^2$ ($n+1=3$) gives a point $p$ in all $D_i$. Then $|p-x_i|\le1$ for all $i$, so all points lie in the unit disk centered at $p$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-10.title: Reduce to three points
dmm-2019-power-10.body:
By scaling the previous problem by the factor $\frac1{\sqrt3}$, it suffices to show that any three of the points lie in a disk of radius $\frac1{\sqrt3}$. (If $k\le2$ the disk of radius $\frac12$ centered at a midpoint works.)

Take three points $P_1,P_2,P_3$ with pairwise distances at most $1$. If the triangle is right or obtuse, the longest side (length at most $1$) is a diameter of a disk containing the third point, radius at most $\frac12<\frac1{\sqrt3}$. If the triangle is acute, its circumscribed disk contains the three points, and its radius is $R=\frac{a}{2\sin A}$ where $a$ is the side opposite the largest angle $A$. Since the angles sum to $180^\circ$, $A\ge60^\circ$, and $A<90^\circ$, so $\sin A\ge\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}2$; also $a\le1$. Hence $R\le\frac{1}{2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2}=\frac1{\sqrt3}$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-11.title: Helly in $\mathbb R^3$
dmm-2019-power-11.body:
Write $s_i=\{x\in S:\langle x,u_i\rangle\ge0\}$ for a unit vector $u_i$, and let $C_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\langle x,u_i\rangle<0\}$, an open half-space, which is convex.

*Claim.* For any set $T$ of indices, $\bigcap_{i\in T}C_i\ne\emptyset$ iff $\bigcup_{i\in T}s_i\ne S$. Indeed if $x\in\bigcap C_i$ then $x\ne0$ and $x/|x|\in S$ lies in no $s_i$. Conversely, a point $y\in S$ in no $s_i$ ($i\in T$) satisfies $\langle y,u_i\rangle<0$, so $y\in\bigcap_{i\in T}C_i$.

If $k\le4$ there is nothing to prove, so let $k\ge5$ and suppose no four hemispheres cover $S$. By the claim any four of the $C_i$ have a common point, so by Helly's Theorem in $\mathbb R^3$ ($n+1=4$) all $C_i$ have a common point; by the claim, $\bigcup_{i=1}^ks_i\ne S$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence some four hemispheres cover $S$. ∎

dmm-2019-power-12.title: Translate the problem
dmm-2019-power-12.body:
Let $Y_i=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:p+K\subset X_i\}$.

*$Y_i$ is convex.* Let $y,y'\in Y_i$, $t\in[0,1]$ and $\kappa\in K$. Then $ty+(1-t)y'+\kappa=t(y+\kappa)+(1-t)(y'+\kappa)\in X_i$ because $y+\kappa,y'+\kappa\in X_i$ and $X_i$ is convex. So $ty+(1-t)y'+K\subset X_i$.

The hypothesis says exactly that any $n+1$ of the sets $Y_i$ have a common point. By Helly's Theorem ($k>n+1$) there is a point $p\in\bigcap_iY_i$, which means $p+K\subset X_i$ for every $i$, i.e. $p+K\subset\bigcap_iX_i$. ∎ (The case $K=\{0\}$ is Helly's Theorem itself.)
